To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the increased freshwater discharge to the coastal zone of a semi-enclosed sea (Baltic Sea) results in a shift in the trophic structure from autotrophs towards microbial heterotrophs.
the increased freshwater discharge suppresses phyto- and elevates bacterioplankton production, thereby increasing microbial heterotrophy and decreasing the trophic transfer efficiency.

the ratio of bacterio-to phytoplankton carbon production (Pb: Pp) is a sensitive indicator of the impact of increased freshwater discharge, and that this indicator can be used to forecast the impact of climate change on coastal food web functioning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of increased freshwater discharge and associated total organic carbon supply on coastal food webs.
the effects of climate change on food web structure in the coastal zone, and the potential consequences for the ecosystem functioning.
the impact of freshwater discharge on the functioning of a coastal food web, and the potential consequences of this for the functioning of the entire ecosystem.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
increased freshwater discharge shifts the carbon flow in the coastal zone towards microbial heterotrophic processes, thereby decreasing the efficiency of energy transfer to higher trophics levels.
increased freshwater discharge shifts the balance between auto-and heterotrophic processes, thereby reducing the efficiency of the transfer of organic matter to higher trophical levels.
climate change is likely to increase microbial heterotrophy in the northern Baltic Sea coastal zone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the coastal zone will be less productive under climate change, with reduced fish production, and reduced sedimentation of organic material to the seabed, a factor of benefit to benthic communities.
increased freshwater discharge shifts the coastal trophic balance towards microbial heterotrophic production.
increased freshwater and organic matter discharge may result in a shift in the trophic structure of the northern Baltic coastal zone towards a microbial-dominated system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
increased freshwater discharge will lead to increased microbial carbon cycling, which in turn will lead to decreased transfer efficiency to higher trophics, and decreased carbon burial.
climate change may have significant consequences for the balance between heterotrophy and autotrophy, and thus the trophic structure, of the coastal zone.

the trophic structure of the northern Baltic coastal zone is sensitive to the input of freshwater and organic carbon, and that the balance between autotrophy and heterotrophy is shifted in favour of the latter with increased freshwater discharge.
